source_reviews.independent_solution: Resolving an individual atom requires spatial detail on the order of 10^-10 m. Visible wavelengths are of order 10^-7 m, and optical diffraction limits a conventional microscope's resolving distance to a scale comparable to lambda/NA, not arbitrary detail obtained by enlargement. Thus ordinary optical magnification cannot resolve atomic dimensions. The reason is the wavelength-dependent resolution limit, not simply brightness, motion or a missing high-magnification lens.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Treat each wavefront element as a secondary-wave source. The observed field at a subsequent point is the superposition of the secondary waves with their amplitudes and phases retained; interference determines the resulting disturbance and intensity. The principle includes both the secondary-wave construction and interference, rather than adding intensities as if the secondary waves were independent.

coverage.evidence: Only q-huygens-fresnel maps to source 2. Every candidate has the wavefront-source clause, and the response distinguishes the complete phase-sensitive combination rule. Loss of writing the principle from scratch is expressly recorded, not concealed as equivalent production.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Principal grating maxima satisfy adjacent-slit path difference=m lambda. At normal incidence this is d sin(theta_m)=m lambda; fixed oblique incidence adds an unchanged incident-angle term. For an actual multi-slit grating, changing N while holding d, lambda and incident direction fixed leaves the principal-maximum angles unchanged. N changes sharpness and, under unchanged per-slit illumination, peak intensity (N^2), not those angular positions.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Use the seed's explicit plane/linear interpretation of polarized light, not an unsupported generalization to every polarization. Natural light has no stable polarization state: transverse statistical mean intensities are equal and orthogonal field components lack a stable phase relationship. Linear polarization has E on one fixed transverse oscillation line and B on a perpendicular fixed transverse line, with both perpendicular to propagation. The field vector may reverse along its line. Rotating E or equal transverse average intensities is not enough to infer natural light, since circular polarization retains a definite inter-component phase relation.

mathematics.independent_solution: A visible-light microscope resolves lengths of order lambda/NA, while an atom is of order 10^-10 m and visible wavelengths are of order 10^-7 m. The mismatch is diffraction-limited resolution, not the ability to magnify the existing image. Post-key comparison: Both author source solutions identify the finite-aperture diffraction resolution limit, reject unlimited magnification and motion-only explanations, and distinguish detail resolution from carrying any position information. Their sets and every declared truth match the frozen independent findings in each locale.

option_checks.evidence: Only absorption is not a valid universal description of an atom's optical response; scattering can carry position information without resolving its outline. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The stated misconception first infers inability to scatter/emit from an unresolved outline, then attributes the missing image to absorption of all incident visible light. That mistaken inference yields the displayed absorption-only claim; the claim is false rather than merely an incomplete correct explanation.

Cooling removes neither visible wavelength nor the diffraction resolution limit; even a stationary atom does not gain a resolved outline. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The stated procedure transfers photographic motion blur to atomic imaging and treats stopping motion as removing every limit. It yields the displayed cooling-to-outline prediction, which remains false under unchanged diffraction resolution.

Visible lambda exceeds atomic dimensions by orders of magnitude, and diffraction prevents an ordinary optical microscope from resolving the requested details. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author derivation uses the correct atomic-size/visible-wavelength comparison and finite-aperture diffraction, with no misconception attached to this true alternative.

Arbitrarily increasing image magnification leaves the object's diffraction-limited spatial resolution unchanged. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Equating enlargement with added spatial information yields unlimited-magnification resolution as displayed. Magnifying a diffraction blur does not add those details, so the recorded procedure genuinely produces a false alternative.

mathematics.independent_solution: Each wavefront element contributes a secondary wave to the observed field. These fields combine with their amplitudes and phases, so equal opposite-phase contributions can cancel rather than add intensities. Post-key comparison: Both author source solutions retain the secondary-wave construction and coherent amplitude/phase sum before computing intensity. Their key and all per-option truths agree with the frozen independent cancellation counterexample and construction checks.

option_checks.evidence: Equal waves in opposite phase yield a zero field, whereas their separately positive intensities have a positive sum. Relative phase cannot be ignored. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Applying the incoherent intensity-sum rule to a common coherent wavefront deletes interference terms and yields the displayed phase-independent intensity sum. Equal opposite-phase waves falsify it.

The wavefront sources and their amplitude-and-phase superposition together provide the Huygens-Fresnel account of the resultant oscillation. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author derivation preserves both wavefront sources and phase-sensitive superposition, agreeing with the independent full principle; its misconception is null.

The field is a sum over secondary contributions, not a nearest-source-only rule; other elements supply interference. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Taking a possibly stronger nearby contribution as the only one deletes the remaining wavefront terms and yields the nearest-wavelet claim. Their interference cannot generally be deleted.

A geometrical envelope without relative phase cannot distinguish interference reinforcement from cancellation at a point. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Treating a drawn envelope as the entire local-field calculation yields the displayed phase-free rule. That rule cannot determine constructive versus destructive interference, so the distractor actually follows the stated omission.

mathematics.independent_solution: Natural-light components have equal transverse mean intensities and no stable relative phase. Linear polarization fixes perpendicular transverse E/B oscillation lines, despite vector sign reversals. Circular polarization rotates E with a definite quadrature phase relation, so rotating direction does not itself imply unpolarized natural light. Post-key comparison: Both author solutions distinguish statistical incoherence from linear fixed axes and circular fixed phase, while retaining E/B perpendicularity. They agree with the independently frozen A/C/F set and all six truths. The option-level B/F contrast was already reviewed before keys as reasonable elimination, not an endorsed answer leak.

E=(E0 cos(omega t),E0 sin(omega t),0) is a rotating vector with fixed component phase difference and definite circular polarization, falsifying the whenever claim. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Generalizing the fixed-line property of linear polarization to every definite polarization classifies rotating E as natural light. That stated overgeneralization yields the displayed universal claim and is falsified by circular quadrature components.

For propagation along z, linear E along x and B along y oscillate on fixed transverse perpendicular lines, exactly as stated. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author correctly obtains fixed perpendicular transverse oscillation lines from linear polarization and the plane-wave field relation.

A linearly polarized sinusoidal field reverses its vector every half-period without changing its fixed polarization line. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Confusing a fixed line with a permanently one-sided vector treats ordinary sign reversal as randomness. It yields the displayed claim and is contradicted by a linearly polarized cosine field.

A vacuum plane wave satisfies B=(1/c) k-hat cross E, so the nonzero instantaneous vectors cannot be independently parallel. Author rationale/misconception comparison: Treating statistically variable orientation as independent electric/magnetic orientations allows a parallel pair as displayed. The vacuum plane-wave cross-product relation excludes that pair for nonzero fields.

Circular polarization has a rotating E vector and a fixed phase relation of the orthogonal components, hence a definite polarized state. Author rationale/misconception comparison: The author correctly preserves the definite relative phase of circular polarization despite rotating direction, matching the independent counterexample to B.
